stimulus.title: Behind the Glass: A Conversation with Paper Conservator Dr. Lin
stimulus.body:
Interviewer: When visitors admire a nineteenth-century watercolour in a gallery, they rarely think about what keeps the paper from yellowing or tearing. What does your work involve?
Dr. Lin: Mostly patience and detective work. Paper made after 1850 often contains wood pulp, which turns acidic over decades and becomes brittle. Before we touch a brush or repair a tear, we test the paper's pH, examine the pigments under ultraviolet light, and document every crease.
Interviewer: What is the biggest misconception people have about conservation?
Dr. Lin: That we try to make old artworks look brand new. In fact, our golden rule is reversibility. Any adhesive we use—such as wheat-starch paste—or any Japanese mulberry paper we attach as a backing must be removable in the future without harming the original sheet. If a future conservator has a better technique, they should be able to undo our repair cleanly.
Interviewer: And what can families do at home to protect treasured letters or drawings?
Dr. Lin: Keep them out of direct sunlight, store them flat in acid-free folders rather than sticky photo albums, and never use ordinary household sticky tape—its glue stains paper permanently within a few years.

workedSolution: Dr. Lin explains that 'Paper made after 1850 often contains wood pulp, which turns acidic over decades and becomes brittle.'
Exam technique: verify 'It frequently contains wood pulp, which turns acidic over time.' directly against the passage and rule out distractors that distort scope or tone.
reviewFocus: Verify passage evidence, Australian English, and absence of defensible distractor readings.

stimulus.title: Two Views: Should Councils Ban Single-Use Coffee Cups?
stimulus.body:
Viewpoint A (Councillor Patel): Every year, Australians discard more than a billion disposable coffee cups. Although many look like plain cardboard, almost all are lined with a thin plastic film that prevents standard paper recycling. A council-wide ban on non-compostable takeaway cups would push cafes and customers to adopt reusable mugs or cup-library schemes, cutting landfill waste immediately. Cities that have introduced small charges or bans have seen reusable cup use triple within six months.

Viewpoint B (Cafe Owner Samira): We all want less litter, but an outright council ban overlooks practical realities. Independent cafes already operate on tight margins, and switching to certified compostable cups costs nearly twice as much per unit—costs that small businesses must pass on to customers. Furthermore, compostable cups still end up in landfill unless the council also invests in commercial composting bins on every street. Incentives for bringing a clean reusable mug—such as a fifty-cent discount—change habits without penalising small shops.

workedSolution: Viewpoint A notes they are 'lined with a thin plastic film that prevents standard paper recycling.'
Exam technique: verify 'They are lined with a thin plastic film.' directly against the passage and rule out distractors that distort scope or tone.
reviewFocus: Verify passage evidence, Australian English, and absence of defensible distractor readings.

stimulus.title: Two Views: Should Councils Ban Single-Use Coffee Cups?
stimulus.body:
Viewpoint A (Councillor Patel): Every year, Australians discard more than a billion disposable coffee cups. Although many look like plain cardboard, almost all are lined with a thin plastic film that prevents standard paper recycling. A council-wide ban on non-compostable takeaway cups would push cafes and customers to adopt reusable mugs or cup-library schemes, cutting landfill waste immediately. Cities that have introduced small charges or bans have seen reusable cup use triple within six months.

Viewpoint B (Cafe Owner Samira): We all want less litter, but an outright council ban overlooks practical realities. Independent cafes already operate on tight margins, and switching to certified compostable cups costs nearly twice as much per unit—costs that small businesses must pass on to customers. Furthermore, compostable cups still end up in landfill unless the council also invests in commercial composting bins on every street. Incentives for bringing a clean reusable mug—such as a fifty-cent discount—change habits without penalising small shops.
